lines.text: Storage returns your bytes intact. Their type decides whether a total, an amount or a timestamp is still right.
Read the four columns on the screen: an id, a status, an amount, a time. Three of them are numbers, and each is a fixed-width box.
That is the thread through this whole topic. The box has a fixed size, the idea inside it does not, and every bug here is the idea spilling out of the box.
Start with the id, because it fails loudest. Thirty-two bits is about two billion distinct values.
Do the arithmetic yourself. A few thousand events every second fills two billion in well under two weeks.
So overflow is not a rare event on a busy table. The only real question is what your system does when it happens.
A thirty-two-bit integer maxes out.
Think about where the arithmetic is running before you answer, because the answer is not a property of the number.
What happens?
It depends on the engine, which is exactly the danger.
Postgres refuses and raises an error. Spark does the same by default since version four.
A numeric array library wraps around to a large negative number and says nothing. Plain Python never overflows, because its integers have no fixed width.
So there is no single right answer to give. That is why code that passes in a notebook can corrupt data in a cluster.
Now the amount, stored as a floating point number. Look at the number line and the tick marks on it.
Each tick is a value the format can represent exactly. Near one they are packed tightly. As the numbers grow, they spread apart.
Past about nine quadrillion the ticks are two apart, so odd whole numbers do not exist there at all.
Add one and you are rounded back to the tick you started on. The sum looks fine and did nothing.
This is the one that catches experienced engineers, so slow down.
One tenth, two tenths and three tenths, added in two groupings. In algebra the grouping cannot matter.
Does it matter here?
Yes. The two totals differ in the last decimal place.
Addition on floats is commutative but not associative. Every step rounds to the nearest tick, and which tick you land on depends on what was already in the running total.
So the grouping decides the rounding. Saying the grouping does not matter is the mathematician's habit, and the machine does not share it.
Now scale that to a million amounts. Watch the two totals disagree.
The error is worst when a large running total swallows a tiny amount whole, the same effect as adding one past the nine quadrillion line.
In a distributed job it gets worse, because the rows of one group arrive from many machines in no fixed order.
So the same query on the same data can return a different total on different runs, and nothing is wrong with the cluster.
The network is not the only thing that reorders a sum.
A vectorized engine adds several values per instruction, so its additions form a wider, shallower tree than a simple loop.
And many cores each build a partial sum, merged in whatever order they finish.
Change the parallelism, and the last digits move. You never wrote a bug. You changed the order of additions.
So how do you get a total that does not depend on order?
Compensated summation keeps the bits that fall off the end of each addition, and shrinks the error a great deal.
An exactly rounded sum goes further and returns one answer in any order. But both are repairs.
The better fix for money is to avoid the binary float, which is the next step.
A fixed point decimal stores cents exactly. There is nothing to round, so there is no drift.
But watch what happens to the digits when you multiply. The scale of the result is the sum of the two scales.
An amount times a tax rate therefore needs more digits than either input. Chain a few of these and you reach the engine's ceiling.
At the ceiling the engine either errors or quietly drops digits. So work out the result's precision before you ship the query, not after.

lines.text: The last number is the time. A timestamp is a count of ticks since nineteen seventy, and the size of the tick is a choice.
Some systems count microseconds. Some older tools count nanoseconds.
Think about what a sixty-four-bit integer can hold, and how big a nanosecond is.
How many years can a nanosecond counter reach, in either direction?
Only about two hundred and ninety years in total, which reaches roughly from the sixteen hundreds to about two thousand two hundred sixty.
A smaller tick buys finer resolution and pays for it in range.
Step outside that window and the counter overflows, so dates far from now need a coarser tick.

lines.text: Now the quiet failure, the one that raises no error.
Write microsecond times to a file, then read them somewhere that rounds to milliseconds. The two integers differ, though they name the same instant.
Join on that column, and rows silently fall out of the result.
A join key has to carry the same tick size on both sides. Pin it explicitly, and never let a default decide.
If you keep one rule from this topic, keep this one: never store currency as a binary float.
Store the cents exactly, in a decimal or as whole minor units. Keep floats for quantities where a tiny relative error is harmless.
That closes the hardware. Next: the algorithms that decide how many bytes a query moves, starting with the two index families most databases are built on.
